description: The seasons do not come from Earth being closer or further from the Sun. The real cause is the tilt of the Earth's axis.

hero.hook: No, summer is not coming because the Earth is getting closer to the Sun.

blocks.text: Many people think that summer comes when the Earth is **closer** to the Sun, and winter comes when it is **far**. This is false. And we see it straight away: when it's summer in France, it's winter in Australia.
The real explanation lies in one thing: the axis of rotation of the Earth is **tilted**, tilted relative to the plane of its orbit around the Sun.

The Earth rotates on its axis in **24 hours**: it is day and night. It also orbits the Sun in **year year** in an orbit shaped like a **ellipse**, a slightly flattened circle. But its axis, the imaginary line from the North Pole to the South Pole, is not straight in relation to its orbit. It leans approximately **23.5 degrees**: this is the . [[Axial tilt of the Earth (23.5°)]]

blocks.caption: The tilt of the Earth's axis explains the cycle of the seasons.

blocks.text: This tilt stays in roughly the same direction all year round. It always points to the same region of the sky, near the North Star. Result: depending on where the Earth is in its orbit, one hemisphere “looks” more at the Sun, the other less.

In summer in the northern hemisphere, the North Pole tilts toward the Sun. The days are longer: the **photoperiod**, the ratio between the length of day and night, increases. The rays also arrive “straight” on the ground: the energy is concentrated on a smaller surface. So it's warmer.

In January, the Earth is even a little **closer** to the Sun than in July: it is the **perihelion**, the closest point in the orbit. And yet, it's winter here. Proof that distance does not explain the seasons.

In winter, it's the opposite: short days, more oblique rays, energy spread over a larger surface. Less heat received. The **solstices**, times when the Sun reaches its northernmost or southernmost position, mark the start of summer or winter.

Near the **equator**, the imaginary line that divides the Earth into two hemispheres, tilt changes little the length of the day. There aren't really four seasons like in Europe, but rather drier and wetter periods.
At **pôles**, the effect is extreme: several months of continuous day in summer, several months of night in winter. The contrast is much stronger there than in France.

If the Earth's axis were perfectly straight, every place would receive roughly the same amount of sunlight all year round. No more real summer, no more real winter. The climate, the cultures, the animal migrations: everything would be different.

The seasons come from the tilt of the Earth's axis, approximately **23.5°**, not from the distance from the Sun. One hemisphere leans towards the Sun: it's summer. The other leans towards the opposite: it's winter.
